query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, the balance between a predominant FCC matrix and a controlled amount of Ni–Al-rich, coherently precipitated ordered B2 (or BCC/B2) phase governs phase stability. The strong negative mixing enthalpy between Ni and Al drives local ordering to form nanoscale precipitates that act as defect sinks and dislocation obstacles, thus simultaneously enhancing high‐temperature strength, radiation tolerance, and preserving cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or homogenized Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy with a single-phase FCC microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a tailored heat treatment (e.g., isothermal hold within 900–1150 °C) or adjust alloy composition (increasing the Ni-to‐Al ratio) to promote the nucleation and growth of a limited, coherent Ni–Al-rich ordered B2 phase within the FCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Processing under well‐controlled thermal conditions where diffusion is sufficient to enable precipitate formation but not so high as to fully transform the matrix. The comparison is made between a baseline alloy retaining a fully FCC structure and an alloy where the designed heat treatment and composition adjustment yields a dual-phase FCC+B2 microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoscale Ni–Al-rich B2 (or ordered BCC) precipitates distributed uniformly within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The strong negative enthalpy of mixing between Ni and Al promotes local chemical ordering, leading to the formation of coherent B2 precipitates. These precipitates hinder dislocation motion (increasing high-temperature strength), serve as defect sinks (improving radiation tolerance), and preserve matrix ductility (maintaining cryogenic toughness). The overall phase stability thus reflects a thermodynamic competition between the entropy‐stabilized FCC phase and the energetically favorable ordering of Ni and Al.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline, a controlled alloy with an optimal volume fraction of coherent B2 precipitates (~small, uniformly dispersed fractions) will exhibit increased high-temperature strength due to precipitation strengthening, enhanced radiation tolerance via defect absorption at precipitate/matrix interfaces, and maintained or even improved cryogenic toughness due to a retained ductile FCC matrix.
generation.baseline: An Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy processed to remain as a single-phase FCC structure under identical conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys with limited composition adjustments (particularly in Ni and Al content) and within thermal processing conditions that permit the onset, but not the dominance, of the ordered B2 phase. Extreme variations in composition or processing that lead to fully transformed microstructures would fall outside the scope.
generation.uncertainty: The exact optimal volume fraction, precipitate size, and distribution of the B2 phase required to achieve the best combination of properties remain to be quantitatively established, and the interplay with other minor elements or secondary phases (such as carbides or oxides) is not fully resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys: one subjected to a heat treatment intended to suppress B2 precipitation (maintaining a single-phase FCC structure) and the other treated to promote controlled Ni–Al ordering (yielding an FCC+B2 dual-phase microstructure). Characterize the microstructure using EBSD, EDS, and XRD to quantify the precipitate fraction and size. Subsequently, test high-temperature mechanical strength, radiation damage resistance (e.g., via ion irradiation experiments with defect density measurements), and cryogenic toughness (through low-temperature tensile tests).
measurements: Phase fraction and precipitate size/distribution (via XRD/EBSD/EDS)
Irradiation-induced defect density and recovery (APT or TEM analysis of defect sinks)
Cryogenic tensile stress-strain behavior and fracture toughness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-phase alloy (with a controlled amount of Ni–Al-rich B2 precipitates) does not exhibit statistically significant enhancements in high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance (lower defect densities or better recovery from irradiation), and cryogenic toughness relative to the fully FCC baseline alloy, then the proposed mechanism of phase stability governing the desirable macroscopic properties via Ni–Al ordering is falsified.

The phase transformations of the Ni36Co18Cr20Fe19Al7 HEA have been studied in this research paper. The alloy underwent hot forging, cold rolling, annealing at and quenching from 1323 K, and isothermal holding, at 873 K. The as-quenched HEA is a single FCC. After the 873-K isothermal holding, the coherent fine L12 particles precipitated homogeneously in the FCC matrix. In addition, cellular precipitation occurred, resulting in the transformation of the high-temperature FCC phase into lamellae of the low-temperature FCC phase and L12 phase. The colonies nucleated and grew from the grain boundaries. The grain boundary moved with the growing tips of the newly formed lamellar FCC and L12 phases, and the lamellar FCC grains had the same orientation as that of one neighboring FCC grain and grew into the other neighboring FCC grain, with a different orientation. The lamellar L12 grains had the following composition: Ni60Co8Cr6Fe6Al20, and the FCC grains had the following composition: Ni31Co15Cr28Fe21Al4. The lamellar L12 phase was rich in Ni and Al, and lean in Co, Cr, and Fe, and the lamellar FCC phase was contrary to this.
